editorial: Title and opening promise a Postgres query p95, but the measured value is the bucket estimate: nearly all calls sit in the 10–50 ms bucket, so the reading of about 48 ms (10 + 0.95×40) would appear for any latency in that bucket. It was 32.1% above the timer's p95, and the post itself says 'the reading tells you the bucket'. Fix: Lead with what the reader can act on: the per-statement mean from _sum/_count, which came within 3.3% of pg_stat_statements, plus the bucket it falls in. State plainly that with the default edges (1, 5, 10, 50 ms...) a p95 near 48 ms means 'between 10 and 50 ms'. Retitle, e.g. 'Postgres Query Latency Per Statement in Splunk From One OTel Java Agent Setting, and the 36-Dimension Budget to Plan For'.

technical: The bucket match offered as proof in the opening could barely fail: a pg_sleep(0.03) statement puts both the timer p95 and the SignalFlow p95 in the 10–50 ms bucket by design, so the match shows bucket placement, not accuracy. Fix: Add a second known statement in a different bucket (e.g. pg_sleep(0.003) for 1–5 ms or pg_sleep(0.07) for 50–100 ms) and show the program tracks it. Otherwise, drop the match as proof in the opening and describe it in the body as a bucket-placement check.

technical: Every latency figure was measured on a node that had run out of CPU credits and had heavy steal, yet those figures appear in the opening and TL;DR while the caveat sits at the end. Fix: Put the credit/steal caveat directly under the p95/mean results and in the TL;DR, or rerun fix.sh on a non-burstable node (e.g. m5.large) so the timer, mean and p95 comparison stands on its own.

editorial: The HTTP section presents an unmeasured explanation ('le would likely make 37') in a way that reads as Splunk not keeping HTTP data, instead of showing the reader how to make room for HTTP percentiles. Fix: Label it explicitly as a hypothesis and reframe it as planning advice: 'To chart HTTP percentiles alongside this, free dimension room first; otel.java.disabled.resource.providers took the agent's resource attributes from 20 to 14 in a short run.' Better, run the main load with the trim and report whether http.server.request.duration_bucket appears.

brief.reader: Platform engineer running Java services on Kubernetes with the OTel Java agent and Splunk Observability Cloud
brief.decision: Whether to turn on the agent's database client metrics across Java services to get query latency charts without touching application code
brief.question: How do I get Postgres query latency from the OTel Java agent into Splunk as a p95 in milliseconds?
brief.takeaway: One environment variable gives you db.client.operation.duration in Splunk on EKS when its series fits Splunk's 36 dimensions per series, and the run shows how close it sits. One SignalFlow program then turns it into a query p95 in milliseconds, with the bucket it falls in telling you how precise that reading is.
brief.adds: The agent's docs name the opt-in, and Splunk's pages cover histograms in general. This post shows the whole path on one running system: the opt-in on the same jar and image, the metric's real series and dimensions in Splunk, and a working SignalFlow program for its p95 in milliseconds.
brief.open_question: With the opt-in environment variable alone on EKS, does Splunk store db.client.operation.duration, how close do its series sit to 36 dimensions, how many series does it hold per Postgres query, what bucket precision do they give, and what query p95 in milliseconds does a Splunk SignalFlow program report at the request rate the load reaches?
tradeoffs: database moves span attributes and pool metrics to the stable names, while database/dup emits both during a move
The stored bucket edges start at 1, 5, 10 and 50 ms, as the le dimension shows them, so a p95 is an estimate inside one bucket
The p95 comes from the histogram's bucket series through SignalFlow, on the Collector chart's default values
